Pico-0: Getting Started with Raspberry Pi Pico

Ethan Rapoport

GE1501 Cornerstone of Engineering 1, Fall 2026

  • Police siren
  • LDR blinker
  • Reversed dimmer
  • RGB rainbow

What is this project?

For Pico-0, I set up a Raspberry Pi Pico with MicroPython and built four breadboard circuits, each controlled by my own mapping in Thonny. I started with two LEDs blinking like a police siren flasher, then added a light sensor (LDR) to make an LED flash in the dark, used PWM to make an LED’s brightness follow the room’s brightness, and finished with an RGB LED that fades through the rainbow, plus a bonus version that translates light level into color on the visible rainbow spectrum.

Goals of the project

  • Challenge 1: Flash two LEDs independently in a police-siren pattern
  • Challenge 2: Make an LED blink like a warning light when the room gets dark, and turn off when it’s bright
  • Challenge 3: Reverse the dimmer so the LED gets brighter as the room gets brighter
  • Challenge 4: Cycle an RGB LED through the rainbow, then make it respond to an LDR by smoothly shifting color and ending on red in the dark

Challenge 1

Police siren

How it’s made

I did all the wiring, learned which resistor corresponds to the LED, and wrote part of the code to control the two LEDs independently. I also had to struggle to get my Pico into the board, because four of its legs are severely bent!

How it works

This was manually coded by telling the LEDs individually to loop a pattern: LED 1 turns on, waits, turns off, then LED 2 turns on, waits, turns off, and it loops, with different wait (time) lengths making it all look like a police flasher, though I couldn’t find a blue LED.

Challenge 2

LDR blinker

How it’s made

I learned to wire an LDR and figure out which resistor goes where, and I also built the code to make the LED flash when it got too dark.

How it works

I first had to measure the LDR’s output for dark by having it print its value constantly. Then I made it so that when the reading drops below a certain value, roughly 14,000, the LED alternates on and off.

Challenge 3

Reversed dimmer

How it’s made

I first built the red LED dimmer, then switched the code around and changed the LED to a different color so it would dim as it got darker.

How it works

I simply made it so that above a certain value, the LED would turn on, and I had the LDR’s value translate as a ratio into the LED’s brightness, updating as often as possible.

Challenge 4

RGB rainbow

How it’s made

At first it was hard to wire the RGB LED, but I figured it out with my classmate’s help: he pointed out I had a resistor in the wrong spot on one of the LED’s pins. After fixing the wiring, I ran the code to cycle colors and generated a program to cycle them smoothly. Then my professor challenged me to create a program that does the smooth cycling based on an LDR sensor, where full dark = red.

How it works

The code treats the RGB LED as three PWM channels (red, green and blue), and set_color sets each one from 0 to 255. I listed the rainbow colors as RGB values and looped through them, holding each for half a second, then using a fade function that takes 100 small steps to the next color so they blend instead of jumping. In the bonus version, the LDR reading picks the spot on the spectrum, with full dark landing on red.

Bonus: Light-controlled color

With an LDR added, the RGB LED shows the room’s light level as a color instead of a brightness, shifting smoothly across the visible spectrum and landing on red at the darkest calibrated reading.
